summary: An informational memo describing the issues and requirements of QoS-based routing and proposing a framework for it in the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: Choosing the best road for traffic based on needs like speed or smoothness, not just distance.

questions: how does qos based routing work
subtitle: Route packets based on traffic quality needs, not just finding the shortest path.

tldr.problem: Today's Internet routing finds the shortest path to a destination regardless of application needs. If an application requires low delay, high bandwidth, or guaranteed performance, the shortest path might not provide it. QoS-based routing is a missing piece of Internet QoS architecture.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a framework where routers compute paths not only on traditional metrics (hop count, cost) but also on QoS metrics (available bandwidth, delay). Within each autonomous system (AS), networks can use innovative QoS routing algorithms; across AS boundaries, a common interdomain protocol facilitates interaction.
tldr.outcome: Networks can offer different service levels to applications that request them. Real-time applications get paths optimized for low delay; bandwidth-hungry applications get wide paths; others continue using best-effort service. This flexibility enables the Internet to support diverse application requirements.

today: RFC 2386 is informational and has not been obsoleted. While the Internet did not fully embrace QoS-based routing as originally envisioned, its concepts profoundly influenced later work including MPLS traffic engineering, segment routing, and quality-of-service provisioning. Many of the issues the RFC identified remain relevant to modern service-differentiation efforts.

sections.title: Beyond Shortest-Path Routing
sections.content:
The Internet's current routing protocols (OSPF, RIP) use shortest-path routing: they compute the path to each destination with the lowest metric (hop count or administrative cost), and all traffic to that destination uses the same path. This approach optimizes for connectivity and simplicity, but not for application requirements.

As the Internet has evolved to support diverse applications—from email (delay-tolerant) to video conferencing (delay-sensitive, bandwidth-hungry) to financial transactions (requiring low jitter)—a one-size-fits-all approach has become limiting. QoS (Quality of Service) mechanisms like IntServ and RSVP allow applications to signal their requirements, but they do not help routers find paths that can satisfy those requirements. A router using traditional shortest-path algorithms cannot route a bandwidth-hungry flow to a different path even if one exists with surplus capacity.

RFC 2386 proposes extending the routing architecture to consider QoS metrics alongside traditional metrics. The goal is not to specify a single algorithm—different networks have different needs—but to provide a framework that networks can build upon.
sections.plainLanguage: Today, routers pick the shortest path like a GPS app. But what if the app also said: I need fast delivery, not just the shortest route? Then the router could pick a different path.

sections.title: The QoS Routing Framework
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a two-level architecture that separates concerns between intradomain (within an AS) and interdomain (between ASs) routing.

Intradomain routing: Within each autonomous system, network operators are free to deploy any QoS-based routing algorithm that suits their needs. Examples include QOSPF (QoS-aware OSPF), which calculates separate paths for different service classes, or more sophisticated schemes that compute multiple candidate paths and select based on resource availability. The RFC imposes no restrictions on these schemes, only that they must be able to interact with a common interdomain protocol.

Interdomain routing: Between ASs, routers need a standardized way to advertise QoS information about paths through their domain so other ASs can make informed routing decisions. The RFC proposes extending the current interdomain routing model (which uses BGP for connectivity) to include QoS information. This allows one AS to tell another: "I have a path to destination X with Y bandwidth available and Z delay."

This separation balances innovation within networks with stability across networks. No two networks need to run the same intradomain algorithm; they only need to speak a common language at the boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network can use its own clever way to pick good paths inside itself. At the borders, they just exchange information about what paths are available and what they're good for.

sections.title: Metrics and Path Computation
sections.content:
QoS-based routing requires metrics beyond hop count. Key metrics include residual bandwidth (unused capacity on a link), delay (propagation and processing time), jitter (variation in delay), and cost (administrative or financial). Different service classes may prioritize different metrics.

Path computation becomes more complex. Computing a shortest path is easy (use Dijkstra's algorithm); computing a path that simultaneously optimizes delay and bandwidth is theoretically harder. The RFC suggests a practical approach: sequential filtering. First, compute paths that meet the primary metric (e.g., minimum delay). From these candidates, filter by the secondary metric (e.g., minimum cost). This trades global optimality for computational simplicity.

The RFC also introduces higher-level admission control: a mechanism to decide whether admitting a new flow is worth the network resources it will consume. Simply finding any path that meets a flow's QoS is not enough; the network should consider: will admitting this flow prevent other, more valuable flows from being admitted later? This fairness problem is especially important for flows requesting large resource reservations.

For multicast routing (one source, many receivers), QoS routing becomes even more complex, since the network must find trees that simultaneously satisfy heterogeneous receiver requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a good path, routers check several things in order: first, is there delay room? Then, is there bandwidth? Sometimes this means saying no to a request, even if a path exists, because accepting it would waste resources other apps need.

sections.title: Intradomain Requirements and Issues
sections.content:
The RFC identifies key issues that intradomain QoS routing must address:

Granularity of routing decisions: Should routing be based on destination address alone (traditional), source AND destination (source-routed), or per-flow (finest granularity, highest overhead)? Each choice affects routing state and complexity.

Metric representation: How are metrics encoded, compared, and accumulated? A path's total delay is the sum of link delays; but what about maximum buffer depth or minimum available bandwidth? These require different aggregation rules. Standards are needed so metrics remain comparable across domains.

Resource availability and reservation: How does a router determine if a link has capacity to serve a flow's QoS requirement? On broadcast media like Ethernet, this is an open problem. On virtual-circuit networks like ATM, the question of which egress points are reachable must be resolved.

Routing oscillations: If QoS-based routing shifts traffic between paths frequently as metrics change, it can introduce instability and variability in delay experienced by end-to-end flows. Mechanisms to dampen updates are needed.

Scalability: QoS routing may generate more routing updates (as metrics change) and require routers to store more state (per-flow, per-service-class). Techniques to manage growth are essential.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to agree on what metrics mean. They need to know if a path really has room for a flow. They need to avoid thrashing—constantly switching paths as tiny network changes occur. And as the Internet grows, all this has to remain manageable.

sections.title: Vision and Evolution
sections.content:
The RFC's ultimate vision is an Internet where QoS-aware routing and resource reservation work together. When an application signals a QoS need through RSVP or a similar protocol, routers can compute a path that is likely to accommodate it, not just the shortest path. Within each AS, operators can innovate; across AS boundaries, a common protocol ensures interoperability.

The RFC acknowledges that no single solution fits all networks. Different operators may choose different intradomain algorithms, different metrics, different admission control strategies. The framework provides the structure for this diversity while maintaining a coherent interdomain model.

Standardization efforts for QoS routing parameters and intradomain protocols were left as future work, allowing the community to experiment and find what works. The framework itself has proven influential in subsequent work on MPLS, DiffServ, and TE (Traffic Engineering) routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to let networks innovate inside their borders while agreeing on how to talk to each other at the edges. This way, everyone can get the service level they need, not just a one-size-fits-all best effort.
